results.title: European force to hold first Ukraine support exercise in Poland
results.description: Around 2,800 troops from 10 European countries will take part in a military exercise in southeastern Poland from November 9 to 22, testing a multinational force designed to support Ukraine after a potential ceasefire. Led by France and Britain, the force aims to bolster Ukraine's security without taking on an offensive role.

results.description: Following the humanitarian mission to Oleshky, Ukraine will establish a separate Center for the Return of Civilian Citizens of Ukraine, which will operate under the Ombudsman's Office.

results.title: Oil rises after report of US strike on Iran's Qeshm Island
results.description: Nov 3 : Oil prices rose in early Asian trade on Tuesday after a report that the United States had struck Iran's Qeshm Island, raising concerns about an escalation of the eight-month conflict and prolonged disruptions to Middle East oil supplies. Brent crude futures rose 48 cents, or 0.5 per cent, to $105.25 a

results.title: Russia Bombs Aid Center And Shelter In Southern Ukraine, Killing 26
results.description: The attacks in the village of Komyshuvakha occurred as a limited ceasefire expired Monday in Kherson, a different region in the country's south.

results.title: Zelensky Confirms Ukraine Retaliated Against Russian Cyberattack by Hacking Moscow’s Emergency Alert App
results.description: President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed in an interview with PBS NewsHour that Ukraine retaliated against a Russian cyberattack on its air raid alert system by hacking Russia’s emergency warning app. The initial attack spread false nuclear and chemical threat alerts across Ukraine.
creator: kyiv post

results.title: Russian strikes kill 26 in Ukraine after longest ceasefire ends
results.description: Russia killed at least 26 people in strikes on a village in southern Ukraine on Monday, including civilians collecting humanitarian aid, emergency workers and police officers. The attack came hours after a rare ceasefire ended, extinguishing hopes of progress towards peace.
creator: france 24

results.title: Russian bombing of Ukrainian aid centre kills at least 26, Kyiv says
results.description: Ukrainian president Zelenskyy says attack on aid hub was ‘vile’ and shows Russia does not want to de-escalate Russia on Monday bombed an aid distribution centre and neighbouring shelter in southern Ukraine, killing at least 26 people, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the country’s emergency services said. Emergency services said two members of a rescue crew and four police officers were among the dead in the village of Komyshuvakha, in south-eastern Zaporizhzhia region. Five people were being treated in hospital, including two rescue workers. Continue reading...

results.title: Rep. Neal: Trump’s move to kick South Africa out of AGOA rooted in ‘grievance’
results.description: President Trump’s move to end trade preferences for South Africa was rooted in a “debunked fixation” on the country’s anti-apartheid efforts, the ranking member of the House Ways & Means Committee charged on Monday, calling on the White House to provide more detail on the decision. Rep. Richard Neal (D-MA), the top Democrat on the House committee with jurisdiction over trade, slammed Trump’s decision to end South Africa’s benefits under the African Growth and Opportunity Act in a Nov. 2 statement, contending the move would reverse economic and social gains made in the program’s 26-year history. “Together, we’ve expanded trade, promoted job creation and worker rights, and strengthened democratic institutions,” he said of U.S. partnerships under AGOA with countries in sub-Saharan Africa. “For the Trump Administration to abandon South Africa and strip them of that progress and opportunity over a debunked fixation on anti-apartheid efforts is unconscionable. It’s yet another trade decision grounded in grievance that flies in the face of what responsible policy should be.” House Ways & Means trade subcommittee ranking member Linda Sánchez (D-CA) similarly contended that the president’s decision was based on his “grievances.” “This isn’t about a trade dispute – it’s about his ridiculous conspiracy theories over apartheid,” she said in an emailed statement. President Trump has made broad, unsupported claims about anti-white racism in South Africa. Bilateral relations also have been strained as a result of the Trump administration’s move to cut foreign aid and because of South Africa’s dealings with Russia and other foreign governments. Concerns about Pretoria’s relations with Russia span both parties and predate the Trump administration. In 2023, then-Senate Foreign Relations Committee ranking member James Risch (R-ID) and panel member Chris Coons (D-DE), along with then-House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Michael McCaul (R-TX) and ranking member Gregory Meeks (D-NY), told Biden administration officials the country's “damaging support” for Russia's invasion into Ukraine raised questions about its eligibility under AGOA. Neal demanded that the White House provide a more fulsome accounting of its decision, which was announced by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative earlier on Monday. “The Administration owes the American people a more thorough explanation as to why South Africa was removed from AGOA and what steps South Africa can take to be reinstated to the program," he said. “Livelihoods, businesses, and U.S. credibility are on the line.” The congressman suggested, too, that the decision was influenced by others around Trump, saying “The power of our trade laws shouldn’t be twisted so Trump can further policies based on biased accusations made by those in his orbit looking to settle scores.” The president's former close adviser and top campaign donor, Elon Musk, who was born in South Africa, has repeatedly accused Pretoria of anti-white racism and has been locked in a dispute with the country over a regulatory demand requiring his company Starlink to surrender part of its ownership to historically disadvantaged groups as a condition to entering the South African market. The Trump administration has asked South Africa to create “alternatives” to the ownership requirement at issue in that dispute, among other demands outlined in a September op-ed by U.S. Ambassador to South Africa L. Brent Bozell. “The South African government now allows all business sectors to participate in [equity equivalent investment programs] but refuses to provide this for the telecommunications or mining industries, where it desperately needs foreign investment. Allow them to participate too,” he wrote. The op-ed addressed a State Department announcement in September on a new visa restriction program targeting certain South African nationals “who are believed to be responsible for, or complicit in, the enactment or implementation of laws or policies that enable uncompensated land seizures, race-based discrimination, and/or the incitement of imminent violence against members of minority ethnic or racial groups in South Africa,” as described by Bozell. He described the visa restriction policy as a “first response” to a failure by Pretoria to address U.S. concerns. “But I won’t pretend it’s the last word either,” the ambassador added. The op-ed does not cite AGOA. Other “asks” that had gone unanswered, according to Bozell, included a demand that the South African president and top officials “condemn the singing of ‘Kill the Farmer! Kill the Boer!,’” an anti-apartheid chant, and for “rural crime” to be “formally designated a priority crime, with a real, announced plan to address it.” By press time, the White House had not issued a statement about the decision to end South Africa’s benefits under AGOA. It deferred questions about Neal’s call for additional information to USTR. A USTR official told Inside U.S. Trade in an email on Monday that the president had sent letters to Congress and South Africa notifying them of his decision. The official also expanded somewhat on concerns set out in USTR’s earlier statement, saying the president had concluded that South Africa was “not making continual progress towards eliminating barriers to U.S. trade and investment and establishing a system to combat corruption.” Further, “certain actions by the Government of South Africa and its relations and cooperation with governments of concern to the United States raise concerns under AGOA’s requirement that beneficiary countries not engage in activities that undermine United States national security or foreign policy interests,” the official said, adding that South Africa “must take meaningful actions to address specific policy and trade concerns.” The official added that the U.S. was “hopeful” for a way forward to address its concerns. An Oct. 28 letter sent by Trump to South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, obtained by SABC News, a South African outlet, outlines concerns similar to those described by the official. In October, South Africa’s ambassador to the U.S. said Washington had refused to provide a clear explanation for how the country could maintain its benefits under the trade program. Bozell, though, said in a social media post on Monday that the president’s decision to end the country’s AGOA eligibility was “a predictable and preventable outcome resulting from the rejection by South Africa's government of real concerns raised by the U.S. Government.” South Africa has been the largest beneficiary of AGOA, shipping about $1.7 billion under the program in 2025, according to data issued by the U.S. International Trade Commission. Those imports included automobiles and agricultural goods, among other products, and represent roughly a tenth of the country’s $16.5 billion in goods exports to the U.S. last year. Like many U.S. trading partners, South Africa also is subject to 12.5 percent tariffs on most of its exports under a Section 301 probe focused on forced-labor trade policies and national security duties on certain goods imposed by the Trump administration. South African Trade Minister Parks Tau on Oct. 30 told reporters that the country would be prepared for any outcome of the eligibility review, according to reports. -- Margaret Spiegelman (mspiegelman@iwpnews.com)
